Gently
jent'ly
adv. (with mildness and care; of the Shepherd leading those with young, and of a king's order concerning a rebel son)
From Latin gentilis, of the same clan, through Old French gentil, well-born — the manner supposed proper to good birth. The Hebrew at Isaiah 40:11 is nahal, to lead to a watering place, to guide with care.

Biblical Definition

Two occurrences carry the word in the Authorized Version, and they are worth setting side by side. The first is a command from a father who is also a king, given about a son in armed rebellion against him: “Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom” (2 Samuel 18:5). It is an order the army heard and disobeyed, and the grief that follows is among the heaviest in Scripture. The second is prophecy of the LORD Himself: “He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young” (Isaiah 40:11). The Hebrew nahal means to lead at the pace the weakest can bear — the ewe heavy with young sets the speed of the flock, not the strong. This comes immediately after the announcement that the LORD God will come with a strong hand and His arm shall rule for Him; the same arm that rules gathers lambs. Gentleness in Scripture is therefore never weakness, but strength governed. The New Testament requires it of ministers — “the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men” (2 Timothy 2:24) — and of any man restoring another taken in a fault.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines gently as softly, meekly, mildly, without harshness or violence.

expand to see more

GENTLY, adv. Softly; meekly; mildly; with tenderness.

2. Without violence, roughness or asperity.

GENTLE, a. Well born; of a good family or respectable birth, though not noble.

2. Mild; meek; soft; bland; not rough, harsh or severe.

3. Tame; peaceable; not wild, turbulent or refractory.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 40:11 — "He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young."

2 Samuel 18:5 — "And the king commanded Joab and Abishai and Ittai, saying, Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom. And all the people heard when the king gave all the captains charge concerning Absalom."

2 Timothy 2:24 — "And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,"

Galatians 6:1 — "Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted."

Modern Corruption

Gentleness is mistaken for mildness of doctrine, so that a man is called gentle when he has merely declined to say anything true.

expand to see more

A widespread confusion identifies gentleness with agreeableness — a manner that avoids conflict by avoiding content. On that account the gentle pastor is the one who never names a sin, and firmness of doctrine is heard as harshness by definition. The text will not support it. 2 Timothy 2:24 puts gentle unto all men in the same breath as apt to teach, and the sentence continues into instructing those that oppose themselves. Isaiah's Shepherd is the same LORD whose arm rules for Him. Gentleness is strength that has taken the measure of the weak and adjusted its pace; a man with no strength to govern is not gentle, only ineffectual.

The opposite error deserves equal attention, since Reformed men are more prone to it. Sound doctrine held without nahal — without leading the flock at the pace the heavy-laden can bear — scatters the very sheep it means to feed. Galatians 6:1 gives the rule for the hardest case: a brother overtaken in a fault is to be restored, and restored in the spirit of meekness, with the restorer watching himself. Joab thought the kingdom was better served by killing Absalom, and he may even have been right about the politics; he was disobeying his king, and the king wept.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nahal, to lead to water, to guide gently — Isaiah 40:11; lat, softly — 2 Samuel 18:5; Greek epios, mild — 2 Timothy 2:24.

expand to see more

Hebrew nahal — to lead to a resting or watering place, at the pace the weak can keep; Isaiah 40:11.

Hebrew lat — softly, secretly, gently; 2 Samuel 18:5, the king's charge concerning Absalom.

Greek epios — mild, gentle as a nurse with children; 2 Timothy 2:24 and 1 Thessalonians 2:7.

Greek prautes — meekness, strength under control; Galatians 6:1, the spirit in which a brother is restored.

Latin gentilis, of the clan — the manner thought proper to good birth, whence English gentle.

Usage

"“Shall gently lead those that are with young” — the flock moves at the ewe's pace, not the ram's."

"“Deal gently… with the young man” — a father's order for a son in rebellion, and disobeyed."

"“Gentle unto all men, apt to teach” — gentleness and doctrine in the same sentence."
